doc.title: Chuck Findley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 6, 2023

title: Close to You versus Nature Boy, and a musical home
summary: The written solo was harder than free improvising on 'Nature Boy'; an artist improvises, classical training is the basis; he grew up on Bobby Hackett records with a musical father and brother Bob.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Man, I mean that one performance sort of encapsulates what you’re capable of with the soloing and the respectful treatment of the melody and then some really high, high notes. So when you think of “Close to You” and that performance is one harder than the other?

I’d say “Close to You” was harder, only because I wasn’t free to improvise on anything like that. It had to be done note by note. Right? I mean on “Nature Boy” I was free to do whatever I pleased to do. So I could — every night I had to play it so I’d play it different every night. You know, it wasn’t that I had to do it — and of course the melody you play but the melody also is not just the melody the way I’d play it the night before. I’d play it differently every night, ‘cause that’s what an artist does or at least what I do anyhow. I mean there are many, many players that play notes you know. Anybody could play the music that’s written in front of them. I mean they could practice and shed you know eight hours a day for all their life and they can’t improvise at all but they can play the notes that are on the paper. That is not being an artist that I consider an artist or a creative person. But the schooling of being a precise player, like you had mentioned, is very, very important. And I recommend that studying classical music is — you need to have that. That’s the basis. You have the basis down and then you go from there. It’s like I played with records and records when I was growing up, and I’d play — Jeez it started with Bobby Hackett. Because my brother was my idol and still is, he’s eight years older than me, my brother Bob, and so I had the cornet, that’s why I started. And Bobby Hackett was the records that I played. My dad was also a wonderful saxophone player and doubled on violin. So we had music in our house all the time, all the time, I mean live music. People would come over and play. So I thought that was the normal, natural thing, people would have these jam sessions, you know?
